concepts.name: Wave optics, the optics of light interacting with small objects
concepts.statement: Wave optics is the branch of optics that considers the behavior of light when it exhibits wave characteristics, particularly when it interacts with objects not much larger than its wavelength, such as a narrow slit. Only waves explain effects such as the colors of a soap bubble or an oil slick.

concepts.name: Interference as the most certain indication of a wave
concepts.statement: A ray passing through slits would continue straight ahead, while a wave spreads out and forms a pattern of bright and dark regions by interference. Such a pattern is the most certain indication that something is a wave, whether water, sound, light or even matter.

concepts.name: The wavelength of light in a medium, λ_n = λ/n
concepts.statement: When light enters a medium its speed drops to $c/n$ but its frequency stays fixed, so its wavelength shrinks by the same factor: $\lambda_n = \lambda/n$.

concepts.name: The frequency and the color of light stay the same in a medium
concepts.statement: Light in a medium behaves like a forced oscillation that keeps the frequency of its source. Its speed and wavelength change, but its color does not, because color is associated with frequency. This keeps the reader from supposing that red light turns blue when it enters water.

concepts.name: Huygens’s principle: every point on a wavefront is a source of wavelets
concepts.statement: Huygens's principle states that every point on a wavefront is a source of wavelets that spread out in the forward direction at the same speed as the wave itself. The new wavefront is a line tangent to all of the wavelets. This one construction explains reflection, refraction and diffraction.

concepts.name: Huygens’s principle explains the laws of reflection and refraction
concepts.statement: The laws of reflection and refraction were stated for rays in the previous chapter. Huygens’s construction shows why they hold: wavelets from a mirror leave in turn and build a wavefront at an angle equal to the incident one, and wavelets in a slower medium travel less far, so the wavefront turns toward the perpendicular.

concepts.name: Diffraction, the bending of a wave around an opening or obstacle
concepts.statement: Diffraction is the bending of a wave around the edges of an opening or an obstacle. Sound fills a room through an open door while light casts a sharp shadow of the doorway, because the amount of bending depends on the ratio of the wavelength to the opening.

concepts.name: Diffraction is greatest for openings about the size of the wavelength
concepts.statement: How much a wave bends depends on the size of the opening compared with its wavelength. A wide opening lets the wavefront through almost straight, and a narrow one spreads it widely. This is the reason light behaves like a ray in everyday life and like a wave in a narrow slit.

concepts.name: Coherent and incoherent light
concepts.statement: Coherent waves are in phase or have a definite phase relationship, and they produce a steady pattern of interference. Incoherent waves have random phase relationships and produce none, as with the two headlights of a car.

concepts.name: Young’s double slit experiment shows that light is a wave
concepts.statement: In 1801 Thomas Young sent light through two narrow slits and found a pattern of many bright and dark lines rather than two lines. The waves from the two slits overlap and interfere, and the experiment gave definitive proof of the wave character of light.

concepts.name: The path length difference from two slits, Δl = d sin θ
concepts.statement: For a distant screen the paths from two slits a distance $d$ apart are nearly parallel, and the difference in their lengths to a point at angle $\theta$ is $\Delta l = d\sin\theta$.

concepts.name: Constructive interference for a double slit, d sin θ = mλ
concepts.statement: Bright fringes of a double slit appear where the path length difference is an integral multiple of the wavelength, $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$. The smaller the slit separation, the larger the angle of each fringe.

concepts.name: Destructive interference for a double slit, d sin θ = (m + ½)λ
concepts.statement: Dark fringes of a double slit appear where the path length difference is a half-integral multiple of the wavelength, $d\sin\theta = (m + \tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$, so that crest meets trough.

concepts.name: The order m of an interference fringe
concepts.statement: The order of an interference fringe is the integer $m$ in the conditions for constructive and destructive interference, the number of whole wavelengths by which its two paths differ. The central fringe is of order zero.

concepts.name: Finding a wavelength or a slit separation from a double slit pattern
concepts.statement: Interference patterns measure wavelength: solving $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ for whichever quantity is unknown gives a wavelength from a measured angle, or a slit separation from a known wavelength.

concepts.name: Finding the highest order of interference possible
concepts.statement: Because $\sin\theta$ can be no larger than one, setting $\sin\theta = 1$ in the interference condition gives the largest order that reaches the screen.

concepts.name: The spacing of fringes on a distant screen, Δy = xλ/d
concepts.statement: For small angles the fringes of a double slit are evenly spaced on a screen a distance $x$ away, with spacing $\Delta y = x\lambda/d$, which grows with the distance to the screen and the wavelength and shrinks with the slit separation.

concepts.name: Coherent light
concepts.statement: Waves are coherent when they are in phase or have a definite phase relationship.

concepts.name: Incoherent light
concepts.statement: Waves are incoherent when they have random phase relationships.

concepts.name: A diffraction grating, many evenly spaced parallel slits
concepts.statement: A diffraction grating is a large number of evenly spaced parallel slits. It forms bright regions at the same angles as a double slit, and gratings work by transmission and by reflection. Opals, butterfly wings and bird feathers owe their colors to natural gratings.

concepts.name: Constructive interference for a grating, d sin θ = mλ
concepts.statement: Each ray from a grating travels $d\sin\theta$ farther than its neighbor, so all of them arrive in phase when $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$, the same condition as for a double slit. The slits of a grating are closer, giving fewer maxima at larger angles.

concepts.name: A grating's maxima are narrower and brighter than a double slit's
concepts.statement: The bright regions of a grating are narrower and brighter, and its dark regions darker, than those of a double slit. The more slits there are, the sharper the maxima, which is why a grating can separate wavelengths that lie close together.

concepts.name: Finding the angles and screen positions of a grating's spectrum
concepts.statement: White light through a grating is spread into a rainbow in every order except the central one, with violet nearest the center. Find the angle of each wavelength from $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ and then its position on the screen from $y = x\tan\theta$.

concepts.name: The single slit diffraction pattern and its broad central maximum
concepts.statement: Light from different parts of one slit interferes with itself. The result is a pattern whose central maximum is wider and much brighter than the dimmer maxima on either side, quite unlike the evenly spaced lines of a grating. The narrower the slit, the more the pattern spreads.

concepts.name: Destructive interference for a single slit, D sin θ = mλ
concepts.statement: A single slit of width $D$ has a minimum where the rays from its top and bottom differ in path by a whole number of wavelengths, $D\sin\theta = m\lambda$, since each ray from one half of the slit then has a partner from the other half that cancels it. There is no minimum of order zero.

concepts.name: Finding a slit width, a wavelength or the angle of a minimum
concepts.statement: Solving D sin θ = mλ gives the width of a slit from the angle of one of its minima, or the angle of any other minimum once the width is known. The same condition applies to sound through a door and ocean waves through a harbor opening.

concepts.name: Diffraction limits the detail an image can show
concepts.statement: Light through a circular aperture spreads into a fuzzy spot surrounded by rings, and the images of two close point sources overlap. Every lens, mirror and pupil has a finite diameter, so this limit to resolution is an inescapable consequence of the wave nature of light.

concepts.name: The Rayleigh criterion, θ = 1.22 λ/D
concepts.statement: By the Rayleigh criterion, two images are just resolvable when the center of the diffraction pattern of one lies on the first minimum of the other. For a circular aperture of diameter $D$ this occurs at $\theta = 1.22\lambda/D$ in radians, so a larger aperture or a shorter wavelength resolves finer detail.

concepts.name: Finding the smallest resolvable separation at a distance, s = rθ
concepts.statement: Once the smallest resolvable angle is known, the distance between two objects that can just be told apart is that angle times their distance away, $s = r\theta$.

concepts.name: Every beam of finite diameter spreads by diffraction
concepts.statement: Even a beam of rays made as parallel as possible spreads out at an angle of about $1.22\lambda/D$ because its diameter is limited. The spreading can be reduced only by making the beam wider, which is why a laser sent to the Moon is first expanded through a telescope.

concepts.name: The resolving power of a lens, x = 1.22 λd/D
concepts.statement: The resolving power of a lens is the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as distinct. The Rayleigh angle with the small angle approximation gives it as $x = 1.22\lambda d/D$, and the smaller it is, the greater the resolution.

concepts.name: Numerical aperture and the resolution of a microscope objective
concepts.statement: A lens with a larger numerical aperture collects more light, gives a brighter image and resolves finer detail: its resolving power is $x = 0.61\lambda n/\text{NA}$. A larger numerical aperture also makes the focal spot smaller, which in wave optics is never a true point.

concepts.name: Thin film interference between light reflected from two surfaces
concepts.statement: Thin film interference is the interference between light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces of a thin film. The ray that enters the film travels farther and may return in or out of phase with the ray reflected at the top, so different thicknesses favor different colors, as in a soap bubble or an oil slick.

concepts.name: A half-wavelength shift on reflection from a medium of higher index
concepts.statement: Light reflecting from a medium with a greater index of refraction than the one it travels in undergoes a 180° phase change, a shift of $\lambda/2$. Light reflecting from a medium of smaller index undergoes none.

concepts.name: Deciding whether a film interferes constructively or destructively
concepts.statement: For light incident perpendicularly, the ray reflected from the bottom of a film travels about $2t$ farther, measured in wavelengths in the film. Combine that path difference with the phase changes at the two surfaces: a total shift of a whole number of wavelengths is constructive, and a half-integral number is destructive.

concepts.name: Designing a non-reflective coating
concepts.statement: A thin layer on a lens can make the light reflected from its two surfaces cancel. When both reflections carry a phase change, the thinnest such coating is a quarter of the wavelength in the film thick, $t = (\lambda/n_2)/4$.

concepts.name: Air wedges and Newton’s rings as fringes of equal thickness
concepts.statement: A film whose thickness changes steadily shows a band of color, or of light and dark in pure light, for every step of one wavelength. Two microscope slides with a hair between them, or a lens pressed on a flat blank, show these bands, which lets a lens be ground to an accuracy of less than a wavelength.

concepts.name: Polarization, the direction of a transverse wave's oscillations
concepts.statement: Polarization is the attribute that the oscillations of a wave have a definite direction relative to its direction of propagation. Light is a transverse wave, and polarized light has its electric and magnetic field oscillations in a definite direction. Only a transverse wave can be polarized.

concepts.name: Unpolarized light and polarizing filters
concepts.statement: A polarizing filter passes only the component of the electric field parallel to its axis, so the light leaving it is polarized. Two filters with crossed axes pass nothing at all.

concepts.name: Malus’s law, I = I₀ cos² θ
concepts.statement: A polarizing filter passes only the component $E\cos\theta$ of a polarized wave's field, and since intensity goes as the square of the amplitude, the transmitted intensity is $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the direction of polarization and the axis of the filter.

concepts.name: Reflected light is partly polarized
concepts.statement: Light reflected from water or glass is partly polarized, more horizontally than vertically, because the vertically polarized part is preferentially refracted. Polaroid sunglasses with vertical axes therefore cut glare.

concepts.name: Brewster’s law, tan θ_b = n₂/n₁
concepts.statement: Brewster's law states that the reflected light is completely polarized when the angle of reflection is Brewster's angle, $\tan\theta_{\text{b}} = n_2/n_1$, where $n_1$ is the index of the medium in which the incident and reflected light travel and $n_2$ the index of the medium that reflects it.

concepts.name: Light scattered by air is polarized
concepts.statement: Sunlight shakes the electrons of air molecules perpendicular to its direction of travel, and they radiate like small antennae, so light scattered at right angles to the original ray is polarized. This is why the blue sky grows bright and dim through rotating polarizing sunglasses.

concepts.name: Liquid crystals, optical activity and birefringence
concepts.statement: Some materials act on the direction of polarization itself. A liquid crystal rotates it by 90° unless a voltage is applied, which is how a pixel of an LCD works; optically active substances such as sugar water rotate it; stressed plastic shows colored patterns between crossed filters; and a birefringent crystal splits a beam in two.

concepts.name: The axis of a polarizing filter
concepts.statement: The axis of a polarizing filter is the direction along which the filter passes the electric field of an electromagnetic wave.

concepts.name: Direction of polarization
concepts.statement: The direction of polarization of an electromagnetic wave is defined to be the direction parallel to its electric field.

concepts.name: Horizontally and vertically polarized light
concepts.statement: Light is horizontally polarized when its oscillations are in a horizontal plane, and vertically polarized when they are in a vertical plane.

concepts.name: Unpolarized light
concepts.statement: Unpolarized light is made of waves that are randomly polarized, with every direction of polarization. The Sun and most other sources produce unpolarized light.

concepts.name: Brewster's angle, $\theta_{\text{b}}$
concepts.statement: Brewster's angle is the angle of reflection at which the reflected light is completely polarized, $\theta_{\text{b}} = \tan^{-1}(n_2/n_1)$.

concepts.name: Optically active substances
concepts.statement: An optically active substance rotates the plane of polarization of light passing through it. Sugar water is an example, and the amount of rotation measures its concentration.

concepts.name: Birefringence
concepts.statement: A birefringent crystal splits an unpolarized beam of light into two beams, which are polarized in different directions.

concepts.name: Reflected light that is completely polarized
concepts.statement: Reflected light is completely polarized when it is reflected at Brewster's angle $\theta_{\text{b}}$.

concepts.name: The wavelength limits the detail a microscope can show
concepts.statement: Because light diffracts around small objects, no microscope using light can show details much smaller than its wavelength. Shorter wavelengths, as in ultraviolet microscopes, show finer detail.

concepts.name: Interference and phase-contrast microscopes enhance contrast
concepts.statement: Light passing through an object of different index emerges out of phase with light from the background, and superimposing the two makes the difference visible as contrast. Interference microscopes and phase-contrast microscopes enhance the contrast of nearly transparent objects in this way.

concepts.name: Confocal microscopes use the extended focal region to image in three dimensions
concepts.statement: A confocal microscope uses the extended focal region of wave optics and a pinhole that blocks light from points out of focus. Scanning the pinhole sideways and then up and down builds a three-dimensional image of a thick specimen, even of live cells in motion.

concepts.name: Contrast
concepts.statement: Contrast is the difference in intensity between objects and the background on which they are observed.

concepts.name: The polarization microscope
concepts.statement: A polarization microscope enhances contrast by using the polarization of light, which makes it useful for objects that are optically active.

concepts.name: The ultraviolet microscope
concepts.statement: An ultraviolet microscope is built with special lenses that transmit ultraviolet rays, and it records its images by photographic or electronic means. Its shorter wavelength shows finer detail than visible light can.

concepts.name: Interference microscope
concepts.statement: An interference microscope enhances the contrast between objects and background by superimposing a reference beam of light upon the light emerging from the sample.

concepts.name: Phase-contrast microscope
concepts.statement: A phase-contrast microscope uses wave interference and differences in phase to enhance contrast.
